c.tagline: Dhow-filled bay town of coconut palms, gateway to Tofo and Barra's whale sharks and manta rays.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hail apps in Inhambane — tuk-tuks and shared chapas (minibuses) handle short hops and the run out to Tofo and Barra; agree the fare with the driver before setting off.

emergency.note: 112 works from mobile phones and connects to emergency services; landline numbers are 119 (police), 117 (ambulance) and 198 (fire).

avoid.reason: Avoid walking Tofo and Barra beaches alone after dark and don't leave belongings unattended — opportunistic theft is the main risk.

hood_desc: The compact historic centre on the bay, with the twin-spired Cathedral of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, an old waterfront mosque, faded Portuguese-era shophouses, the jetty and market; the walkable base for exploring the town's colonial and dhow heritage.

The famous surf-and-dive beach 22 km east, a long stretch of powdery sand backed by dune bars, dive centres and seafood shacks; the lively, social base for whale-shark and manta diving and Inhambane's nightlife.
A palm-backed sand spit at the peninsula tip with calm, shallow flats, a mangrove estuary and low-key beach lodges; a quieter, family-friendly base for snorkelling, kite-surfing and long walks.
The rocky headland and surf point just south of Tofo, with a sacred cliff, tidal pools and a handful of relaxed lodges; a calmer, scenic alternative to the main Tofo strip.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap supply is unreliable.

transit.hours: Chapas and tuk-tuks run from around dawn until early evening; after dark, tuk-tuks and pre-arranged taxis are the main way to get around.
transit.note: Inhambane has no formal public transport; getting around means shared chapas (converted minibuses) and tuk-tuks around town and out to the beaches, plus dhows across the bay to Maxixe.
transit.pay: Pay the chapa conductor or tuk-tuk driver in cash (roughly 15-50 meticais a hop; more for Tofo/Barra); dhow crossings are a few meticais. Carry small notes.

bus: Long-distance buses to Maputo & Vilanculos (from Maxixe)
ferry: Dhows and motor ferry across the bay to Maxixe

transit.m: Tuk-tuk or taxi to the town centre (5-10 min)
Chapa (shared minibus) toward the town centre

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving ~10% at tourist restaurants and for dive/tour guides is appreciated where service isn't already added.

landmarks: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Conception (old cathedral)
An 18th-century whitewashed Portuguese cathedral whose weathered bell tower rewards climbers with sweeping views over Inhambane Bay.
Ponta da Barra and Barra Lighthouse
A palm-backed peninsula where the bay meets the Indian Ocean, its lighthouse and dune-fringed beaches ideal for sunset walks.
Mercado Central de Inhambane
A lively covered market piled with cashews, tropical fruit, capulana fabrics and fresh fish, the fragrant heart of daily Inhambane life.
Old Mosque of Inhambane
A modest 19th-century mosque testifying to centuries of Swahili and Arab trade in one of Mozambique's oldest coastal settlements.
Inhambane Railway Station and jetty (Ponte-cais)
A charming colonial-era station and long wooden pier where dhows glide past, evoking the town's heyday as a trading port.
Provincial Museum of Inhambane
A small but engaging museum of ethnographic treasures, musical instruments and colonial relics telling the story of Inhambane province.
Dhow crossing to Maxixe
The classic Inhambane experience, sailing a traditional wooden dhow across the sparkling bay to the market town of Maxixe.
Guinjata Bay and Jangamo beaches
A string of wild, reef-fringed beaches south of town where divers explore Manta Reef's cleaning stations and deserted sands.
Ilha dos Porcos (Pig Island)
A tiny bay island reached by dhow, offering sandbank picnics, birdlife and clear shallows within sight of Inhambane's waterfront.
Cine Teatro
A weathered Art Deco cinema in the old town, one of the few surviving examples of Inhambane's 1940s Portuguese colonial architecture.

train.note: Inhambane has no working railway. The short colonial-era line that ran inland from Inhambane towards Inharrime closed long ago and the province is served only by the EN1 highway. Mozambique's surviving passenger trains are elsewhere - CFM's Maputo suburban services and the northern Nacala corridor train between Nampula and Cuamba, continuing to Lichinga (https://www.cfm.co.mz/). No passenger train crosses any Mozambican border, so rail is not an option for reaching Inhambane.

bus.note: Most long-distance transport leaves from Maxixe, across the bay: chapas and buses run down the EN1 to Maputo (~7-8 hrs) and north to Vilanculos. Local chapas connect Inhambane town to Tofo and Barra.

intl.op: local dhow and motor-ferry operators — tickets at the jetty

ferry.note: Wooden dhows and a small motor ferry shuttle across the bay between Inhambane's jetty and Maxixe throughout the day (~30 min), the quickest link to the mainland highway.

half.blurb: A legendary dive beach 22 km east, famous for year-round whale sharks, reef manta rays and coral reefs, plus dune bars and a lively backpacker scene.

half.name: Barra

full.blurb: The bustling mainland market town across the bay, reached by a short dhow or ferry ride and the region's main transport hub.
full.name: Maxixe
